Cunningham had run office work for the Development Projects Division, the unit behind the U-2 and the Cuba air effort. The excerpt kept here centers on a dry but sharp dispute: what time did the bombers really take off?

Cunningham walks through rival mission logs. One shows pilot Herrera leaving alone at 0700Z. A later fix by Gar Thorsrud moves Doug Price's takeoff beside Connie Seigrist's. A book on the landing had stirred the fight, and the Taylor Committee had used one version. The talk shows how hard the basic facts were to pin down.
un-ga-res-a-69-66:
Half the world has already banned nuclear arms from its soil, and Resolution A/69/66, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, marks that fact. Any group of states may make a pact to keep such arms out of its lands in full. That right stands in the 1968 pact against the spread of nuclear arms. Five zone pacts are named with praise, from Latin America to Africa and the Pacific.

With the Antarctic Treaty, those pacts have freed the whole southern half of the world, and the seas beside it, from nuclear arms. Mongolia's own lone-state free status is recalled as well. Till such arms end for good, the text holds, zones of this kind are a firm step toward that end.
un-sc-res-266: A formal decision of the United Nations Security Council, Resolution 266 is catalogued here under 1969. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1666: Security Council Resolution 1666, issued in 2006, comes to the collection through the official record held by English Wikisource. un-sc-res-1866: Resolution 1866, from 2009, is a formal Security Council decision preserved in official-record form via English Wikisource. un-sc-res-1966:
War crimes courts need an ending plan, and Resolution 1966, adopted in December 2010, created one. The tribunals for Yugoslavia and Rwanda were finishing their trials. The Council set up a residual mechanism to carry on their leftover duties for years afterward.

The new body tracks fugitives, protects witnesses, guards the archives, and can retry or refer cases as needed. It has branches in Arusha and The Hague, matching the two courts it serves. The text matters because justice for mass crimes does not end with the last big trial, and someone must keep the record.
cia-0000132766:

Property fights mattered because they turned ideology into losses that businesses and newspapers could count. Each takeover pushed the two governments further apart that summer. The briefing, one of two Cuba papers dated June 4, tracks the early-summer radicalization that made a break hard to avoid. It survives through the CIA Reading Room, mirrored online by the Internet Archive.

un-sc-res-166:
Security Council Resolution 166, adopted on October 25, 1961, recommended Mongolia for membership in the United Nations. Mongolia had sought a seat since 1946, but Cold War bargaining kept its bid blocked for fifteen years. A package deal that year, which also cleared Mauritania, at last let the landlocked Asian state through the council.

The General Assembly admitted Mongolia two days later. The text follows the standard form for new members: the council finds the applicant peace-loving and able to carry out the Charter, then passes the choice to the Assembly. For Mongolia, the vote ended a long wait at the door of world politics.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d66: Edward Stettinius, the Acting Secretary of State, wrote to President Roosevelt on October 28, 1943, while Hull was still abroad. The record names the parties and the date. Its business is stated only in the printed Foreign Relations text.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d166: British members of the Moscow Conference's committee on Iran wrote a memorandum dated October 25, 1943, preserved as Document 166 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The memorandum is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d266:
The foreign callers who visited President Roosevelt at Cairo on the afternoon of 24 November 1943 are listed in an editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume. The names come from the President's Log, with additions from Admiral Leahy's account, and the calls appear to have been brief and mainly courteous in nature.

Egyptian leaders came first, then King George II of Greece with Prince Paul, British commanders from Egypt, and King Peter II of Yugoslavia with his prime minister. Leahy adds Turkey's prime minister and Britain's ambassador to Turkey. No memoranda were made of any of the talks. King Peter's own book later described his conversation, which ranged over reconciling Tito and Mihailović and the case for Allied landings on a fixed date.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d366:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the second plenary session at Tehran, on 29 November 1943 at four in the afternoon. With no set agenda, Roosevelt calls for reports from the military staffs who had met that morning, and Brooke, Marshall, and Voroshilov speak in turn.

Brooke reports the committee ranged over Italy, Yugoslav aid, Turkey and the Dardanelles, a southern France operation alongside Overlord, and the bombing of Germany, without finishing its work. Marshall stresses that landing craft, above all those carrying forty tanks, are the choke point, while a million tons of supplies already sit in England on schedule. Then Stalin asks who will command Overlord. Told it is undecided, he warns that nothing will come of the operation unless one man is made responsible for both its preparation and its execution.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d466:
Secretary of State Cordell Hull cabled President Roosevelt on December 2, 1943, while the President was traveling between the Tehran and Cairo conferences. Hull had stayed in Washington, so the State Department's part in the summit season ran through messages like this one. The cable appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Hull was the administration's senior diplomat, fresh from the Moscow foreign ministers' meeting that had prepared the way for Tehran. His cables kept the traveling President tied to the department and to the questions waiting at home. For readers, the message shows how much of wartime diplomacy was done by wire, across thousands of miles.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d566:
Harry Dexter White wrote this third memorandum on September 13, 1944, while the Second Quebec Conference was meeting. White's Treasury work fed directly into that conference, where the treatment of postwar Germany was fiercely debated. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

A White paper dated during Quebec sits close to one of the war's most argued episodes: the Morgenthau Plan for Germany's economy, which the Treasury championed and others resisted. Readers should treat the date and desk as the story here. The memorandum shows staff work arriving at a summit in real time, as the economic peace was fought over.
frus-1944-quebec-d66:
President Roosevelt addressed this message to Secretary of the Treasury Henry Morgenthau on September 12, 1944, the opening day of the Quebec Conference. Morgenthau had come to Quebec with the plan for Germany that bears his name. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Morgenthau proposed stripping Germany's industry to keep it harmless, a plan that split the American government and startled the British. A presidential message to him on day one sits at the center of the conference's most famous controversy. For readers, it is a direct thread to the Morgenthau Plan episode, told from inside the President's own party.
frus-1944-quebec-d166:
Operations for the defeat of Japan in 1944–45 are scheduled in C.C.S. 417/8, issued by the United States Chiefs of Staff on September 9, 1944. The agreed objective was Japan's unconditional surrender, forced by blockade and bombardment and by invading her industrial heart. The paper lays out a dated course of action for planning across the Pacific.

The schedule runs from Talaud in October 1944 through Leyte that December, then Formosa or Luzon in early 1945. The Bonins, Ryukyus, and the China coast follow, with southern Kyushu in October 1945 and the Tokyo Plain in December. Every effort, it adds, should bring the Soviet Union into the war at the earliest practicable date. Events overtook several target dates during the conference itself.
frus-1944-quebec-d266:
C.C.S. 676, presented September 12, 1944, compiles the area commanders' reports on Pacific operations from November 1943 to September 1944. In the Central Pacific, amphibious forces had successively taken the Gilberts, including hard-defended Tarawa, then the Marshalls, then Saipan, Tinian, and Guam in the Marianas. The Palaus operation was scheduled for September 15.

The report records the Philippine Sea engagement, where carrier aircraft inflicted severe damage on the Japanese fleet during the Marianas operation. It praises the submarine campaign's heavy toll on Japanese shipping. The Marianas, it notes, offered bases for very-long-range bombers against Japan proper, with preparations underway at full speed. Northern Pacific operations were limited to raids on the Kuriles.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d66:
Harry Hopkins, the President's special assistant, sent this light personal report from London on 24 January 1945. It is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. Hopkins was traveling ahead of Roosevelt and had just met Churchill.

Hopkins calls his London visit very satisfactory and says he leaves for Paris the next day. He passes on Churchill's joke that ten years of research could not have found a worse place than Yalta. Churchill planned to survive it with plenty of whisky, which he claimed was good for typhus and deadly on lice. Hopkins ends with word that Watson was seasick as usual.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d166:
Rebuilding Poland and the Balkans gets a cool cost-and-politics survey in this briefing book paper. Prepared for the President's trip, it is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Its summary weighs American interests against the Soviet attitude, and finds one of the two easy to state.

American trade interests are general: an early return to many-sided trade, and a stable, thriving Europe. In politics, Washington probably would not fight a chief Soviet influence in the area, but it would not want its own voice wiped out. The needs are plain: better farm methods, rebuilt railways, new rolling stock, mended roads and bridges. American help would flow through Export-Import Bank credits, farm experts, and the proposed International Bank.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d266:

Andrew Lang, the Scottish folklorist and man of letters, published Myth, Ritual, and Religion in 1887 as his manifesto in the science of religion. Lang opposed Max Muller's school, which read all myth as a disease of language about the sun. He argued from custom instead.

Lang holds that the savage rites and beliefs of living peoples explain the strange, irrational parts of Greek and other myths: the myths are fossils of ritual ages. He ranges over totemism, sacrifice, and the making of gods. The book is the anthropological school's classic statement, complete, and a model of learned argument written with a storyteller's ease.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ClarkRamseyExec:
On October 31, 1966, Attorney General Ramsey Clark issued this order on the physical evidence of the Kennedy assassination. Acting under Public Law 89-318, it provides for the United States to acquire and preserve the items of evidence pertaining to the assassination.

The order was the legal hinge on which the autopsy materials and other exhibits passed into the National Archives under controlled custody. Preservation sounded simple; in practice it set off decades of argument over access, since the same law that saved the evidence also fenced it. The order is preserved as the founding document of the assassination archive's custody.
drake-witchcraft-delusion-vol1-1866:
Samuel Gardner Drake, a Boston antiquarian and bookseller, built his Witchcraft Delusion in New England around two famous Salem-era books. Volume one, issued in 1866, reprints Cotton Mather's Wonders of the Invisible World in full. Mather first published that defense of the trials in 1693, while the Salem hangings were still fresh.

Mather, a leading Boston minister, wrote to prove the trials were just and the threat was real. Drake adds his own preface, opening essay, and notes to set the scene. Readers get the case for the prosecution in its own strong words. The volume pairs a key source with a guide to its world.
drake-witchcraft-delusion-vol2-1866:
Volume two of Drake's Witchcraft Delusion in New England answers volume one. Where the first volume gave Cotton Mather's case for the Salem trials, this 1866 volume reprints the reply. Its author was Robert Calef, a Boston merchant with no love for the Mathers.

Calef's More Wonders of the Invisible World, first printed in 1700, charges that ministers and judges fed the Salem panic. He retells cases, prints letters, and questions the proof used to hang men and women. Drake's notes frame the feud for later readers. The book stands as the first close, on-the-spot attack on the trials.
drake-witchcraft-delusion-vol3-1866:
Volume three closes Samuel Drake's three-volume Witchcraft Delusion in New England, printed in 1866. The set reprints the great books of the Salem era with Drake's prefaces and notes. This last volume carries the story past Mather's defense and into the long argument that followed.

Its pages hold further tracts and records from the New England witchcraft years. Read with the first two volumes, it fills in names, cases, and charges the famous books leave out. Drake meant the set to serve as a working archive, not a tale retold. Together the three volumes give the trials and their fallout in full.
chelmsford-witches-examination-confessio:
Printed in 1566, The Examination and Confession of Certaine Wytches at Chelmsford holds a first in English print. No earlier English pamphlet on a witch trial is known to survive. The Essex assizes town of Chelmsford gives the case its name.

The pamphlet sets out the questioning of the accused women and the confessions said to follow. Its plain question-and-answer shape set the pattern for scores of trial pamphlets after it. Readers see the charges grow out of sick beasts, spoiled goods, and neighborly spite. The small book opens two centuries of English witchcraft in print.
walsh-examination-dorchester-1566:
John Walsh of Dorchester was called before a church court officer in 1566 to answer claims of sorcery. The Examination of John Walsh preserves that rare early session in print. Most later witch cases went to crown courts, but Walsh faced church discipline instead.

Question by question, the record shows how a lone man said to work magic was handled. The officers probe his books, his charms, and the help he gave his neighbors. No gallows waits at the end of this story, and that sets it apart. The pamphlet catches the years before the great witch panic took hold.
ufo-hearings-house-1966:
Congress called the Air Force to account on UFOs in the spring of 1966. The House Committee on Armed Services held its hearing on April 5, with the public and press at full attention. A wave of sightings over Michigan that March had forced the issue.

The astronomer Allen Hynek, the Air Force's own adviser, told the panel the subject deserved true science at last. Generals laid out the Blue Book files and held that most cases had plain causes. The hearing pushed the Air Force to seek an outside study. From that push came the Condon study and the end of Blue Book.
duncan-masonic-ritual-1866:
Malcolm C. Duncan put out his Masonic Ritual and Monitor in 1866. The book prints the rites of the craft lodge in full. It runs from the first grade, Entered Apprentice, up to Royal Arch. Duncan wrote for Masons and for the keen man in the street.

Signs, grips, oaths, and floor work stand in plain print, grade by grade. Cuts show the lodge room, the tools, and the dress of each rank. Past books had hid the rites; Duncan sold them to all. The work is still the stock guide to the craft rites of its age.
cavendish-blazing-world-1666:
Margaret Cavendish wrote The Blazing World in 1666. Cavendish was Duchess of Newcastle and a bold mind of her age. The work tells of a lady stole by sea thieves and swept by storm to the north pole. A door at the pole leads her to a new world.

Beast men of all kinds serve her as she weds the lord of that world. She talks with spirits on God, stuff, and the soul at great length. She then leads a fleet back to aid her own land in war. The work is one of the first tales of its kind in English.
baring-gould-curious-myths-first-series-:
Sabine Baring-Gould was a priest and scribe of vast range in Devon. His Curious Myths of the Middle Ages, First Series, came out in 1866. The book digs up the odd tales the mid ages loved most. A Second Series came after to round out the set.

The Wandering Jew, William Tell, and the man in the moon all get a look. Baring-Gould traces each tale to its root and weighs how it grew. His tone is warm, keen, and full of lore from old books. The book is still a joy for fans of the myths of the folk.
thoreau-yankee-in-canada-1866:
Henry David Thoreau's A Yankee in Canada saw print in 1866, after his death, a posthumous collection. The volume joins the Canada travel tale with his Anti-Slavery and Reform Papers in one last book. Slavery in Massachusetts, Life Without Principle, and Wendell Phillips stand among its fierce reform pieces in print.

Thoreau toured Quebec in 1850 and found old French Canada quaint, priest-ridden, and unfree in its own way. The travelogue mixes soldier lore, cathedral visits, and St. Lawrence scenery with his Yankee skeptic's dry wit throughout. Slavery in Massachusetts, his angriest speech, damns his state for returning fugitives under federal law in 1854. Life Without Principle scorns the money chase and calls work a form of prayer when freely chosen. The set shows Thoreau the reformer beside Thoreau the walker, one pen, two fires.
bunyan-grace-abounding-1666:
John Bunyan was a tinker and lay preacher in Bedford. In 1666 he wrote Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, as he faced prison for preaching without a license. The book tells, in plain and searching prose, how he came to settled faith. It is the classic Puritan conversion narrative.

Bunyan recounts years of despair, in which Bible verses struck him by turns as promise and as threat. He describes his fears of having sinned beyond pardon and the slow peace that followed. Later readers, from Wesley onward, treated the book as a map of the troubled conscience.
westcott-gospel-resurrection-1866:
Brooke Foss Westcott, the Cambridge scholar who later became bishop of Durham, published The Gospel of the Resurrection in 1866. The book began as essays on the meaning of Easter for faith and life. Westcott treats the resurrection not as one doctrine among many but as the center.

He argues that the risen life of Christ reshapes how believers read history, nature, and their own deaths. His method joins close Greek study to wide meditation on the church's worship across the ages. Victorian readers found in Westcott a learning that prayed, and the book shaped Cambridge theology for decades.
baring-gould-curious-myths-1866:
Sabine Baring-Gould, an English clergyman and folklorist, published Curious Myths of the Middle Ages in 1866. Baring-Gould collected strange tales that medieval people told and believed. Each chapter takes one myth and traces where it came from and how it changed.

Stories include the Wandering Jew, Prester John, the Seven Sleepers, and other saints' tales and wonders. Baring-Gould compared versions across lands and languages to find the root of each tale. He wrote as both a believer in old lore and a careful scholar of it. The book helped start the modern study of folklore and shows how myths travel and grow.
swinburne-poems-ballads-1866:
Algernon Charles Swinburne published Poems and Ballads in 1866, a year after Atalanta in Calydon made his name. The new book scandalized Victorian England. Reviewers attacked its passion and paganism so fiercely that the first publisher withdrew it, and another quickly took it up.

Dolores, a hymn to a cruel goddess of pain, leads the notorious pieces. The Garden of Proserpine imagines death as peaceful sleep beyond love and weariness. Other poems praise Sappho, freedom, and the sea in rushing, musical lines. Swinburne's technique dazzled even his enemies. The volume, complete in its first series here, made him the wild star of late Victorian poetry.
whittier-snow-bound-1866:
John Greenleaf Whittier published Snow-Bound in 1866, just after the Civil War, and it made him financially secure at last. Whittier set the long poem in his boyhood home in Haverhill, Massachusetts, remembering a great snowstorm that sealed the farmhouse for days. He dedicated it to the family circle it describes, most of them by then dead.

As the storm rises, the family gathers at the hearth: father, mother, uncle, aunt, brother, sisters, a schoolmaster boarder, and a storytelling guest. Each portrait is drawn with tender exactness, and the firelight holds off the cold and the reader's knowledge of loss. Whittier called it a winter idyll. It became the great American fireside poem and his most perfect work.
lessing-laocoon-1766:
Gotthold Ephraim Lessing published Laocoon in 1766, and Ellen Frothingham translated it into English in 1873. The essay takes its name from the famous statue of the priest Laocoon and his sons in the grip of sea serpents. Lessing asks why the statue's pain looks so different from pain in poetry.

His answer draws a famous line: painting and sculpture work in space, poetry works in time. Each art, he argues, fails when it tries to do the other's job. The argument reshaped how critics in Europe judged both arts. Laocoon became the founding text of modern aesthetics, the study of how art works. Its clear reasoning still anchors debates about image and word.
kardec-evangile-selon-le-spiritisme-1866:
Allan Kardec made L'Evangile selon le spiritisme the third book of his Spiritist canon in 1866. The text here is the Paris third edition of that year, revised and corrected. Kardec reads the moral maxims of Christ through Spiritism, his system of spirit teaching. Each saying receives an explanation drawn from mediums' messages.

Charity, forgiveness, and humility form the core of the teaching. Kardec presents the book as moral guidance for daily life. No nineteenth century English translation exists, the first coming only in 1987. The French text therefore stands as a documentary edition. Spiritists still treat this volume as their gospel companion. Its order is calm and didactic.
davis-death-after-life-1866:
Death and the After-Life, from 1866, gathers three discourses by Andrew Jackson Davis. Davis, the Poughkeepsie Seer, taught that death is a birth into a higher sphere. His name for the spirit world was the Summer Land. The discourses give his core statement of the spiritualist afterlife.

He describes the process of dying as his clairvoyant sight reported it. The spirit leaves the body by stages, then wakes among scenes of the after life. Friends and guides greet the new arrival in his telling. Comfort for mourners runs through every page. The small book carried his teaching to a wide audience. It stays a key spiritualist text.
lippe-text-book-of-materia-medica-1866:
Adolph Lippe stood for the strictest reading of Hahnemann, and his Text Book of Materia Medica of 1866 shows that stance on every page. Lippe listed the drugs homeopaths used, with the signs that point to each one. He trusted the proving record and little else.

For each remedy he stresses the characteristic symptoms, the odd, clear signs that mark it off from all others. His practice used one remedy at a time, often in very high potencies. Students of the strict Hahnemann school still read Lippe as the purest guide to that way of prescribing.
plos-pone-0003466:
Borja Guerra and co-authors compared hunger signaling in men's and women's muscles in this 2008 study. Leptin is a hormone that reports body fat stores to tissues. It docks at receptors found on skeletal muscle. The team measured receptor forms, blood leptin, and insulin sensitivity by sex.

They also checked a brake protein called SOCS3 in the muscle. Levels differed between men and women in several of these measures. Such sex gaps may help explain unlike patterns of metabolism. They could also bear on why diabetes risk differs by sex. Muscle is a major user of blood sugar, so these gaps carry real weight.
plos-pone-0003566:
Marie Forgeard and co-authors linked childhood music practice to wider skills in this 2008 study. They asked whether instrumental training in childhood relates to other abilities. Some outcomes sit close to music, others far from it. Children with at least three years of training were studied.

That trained group outperformed peers on verbal ability tests. They also scored higher on nonverbal reasoning. The average training length was about 4.6 years. Sustained practice may sharpen powers well beyond music itself. Music training is common in childhood, so wide effects would touch many lives.
plos-pone-0003666:
Joan Y. Chiao, Nicholas E. Bowman, and Harleen Gill published this psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Men hold most top political posts, even where any elected person may serve. The team asked whether quick judgments from candidates' faces feed that gap.

Voters' snap reads of faces predicted how they voted in the study. Those same reads tilted by the candidate's gender, favoring some looks in men and others in women. The study shows a facial bias in voting that may help keep political power uneven between the sexes. The work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008.
plos-pone-0003766:
Alexander Vogt, Cecilia D'Angelo, Franz Oswald, and colleagues published this protein study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Fluorescent proteins from sea creatures are standard markers for filming living cells. Demand for better imaging keeps driving the search for new ones with fresh properties. The team found one in the deep sea.

Their green fluorescent protein can be switched on and off with light. That photoswitchable emission lets researchers highlight and track chosen molecules in a cell. The marker gives cell biologists a sharper tool for live imaging than always-on proteins allow.
plos-pone-0003866:
Eva Terzibasi, Dario Riccardo Valenzano, Mauro Benedetti, and colleagues published this aging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The annual fish Nothobranchius furzeri lives fast and dies young, making it a handy model for aging research. One inbred lab strain shows exceptionally short life and fast-rising age markers.

The team analyzed new wild-derived lines of the species in captivity. They characterized survival and age-related traits in each line. Large differences in aging phenotype appeared between strains, a range that turns this tiny fish into a sharper tool for studying why organisms age.
plos-pone-0003966:
Lihua Tan, Paul Schedl, Ho-Juhn Song, and co-authors used fruit flies to trace Alzheimer's damage in 2008. Alzheimer's disease slowly destroys memory in many older people. A short protein piece called Abeta42 is directly implicated in it. Which genes and paths carry its harm stayed unclear.

Their PLOS ONE article reports the Toll to NF-kappaB path carries that harm in flies. That path is better known for fighting infection in the body. Finding it in brain damage links immunity and Alzheimer's in a new way. Fly results can guide which paths to check in human tissue.
plos-pone-0004066:
Solène Mine, Nicolas O. Fortunel, Hervé Pageon, and co-authors compared two skin cell types across aging in 2008. Skin strength rests on the dermis, the layer under the surface. The dermis holds two fibroblast types, papillary and reticular. Their separate roles in aging were poorly understood.

Their PLOS ONE article used matched cell pairs from the same donors. Aging changed papillary fibroblasts in function, but not reticular ones. That split view revises how skin aging is described. Treatments may need to target one layer's cells, not skin as a whole. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004166:
Harry Courtney and colleagues published this microbiology study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Streptococcus pyogenes is a bacterium that causes strep throat and more serious infections. Its surface is water-repelling, a trait that helps it stick to surfaces and form biofilms. That trait comes mainly from lipoteichoic acid held on the cell surface.

How that acid stays anchored was not well understood. The team tested how the family of M proteins relates to this acid and to biofilm growth. M proteins are key surface proteins of the bacterium. Their findings tie the bacterium's grip and film-forming habits to specific surface parts.
plos-pone-0004366:
Philip Gingerich and colleagues published this fossil whale study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Protocetids are middle Eocene archaeocetes, predators ancestral to later whales, living 49 to 37 million years ago. They are found in marine rocks but retain four legs and were not yet fully aquatic. They are interpreted as amphibious animals that fed in the sea but returned to land, perhaps to rest and give birth.

The team describe a new protocetid whale from the middle Eocene of Pakistan. Their evidence covers birth on land, precocial development, and sexual dimorphism. The fossil fills a step in the whale's long route from land back to sea.
plos-pone-0004466: In 2009, Sone, Uchida, and Komatsu found a gene guiding protein delivery. Loss of yata, a novel gene, mislocalized APPL and harmed young fly brains. The delivery gene's absence scrambled transport. The finding maps neural trafficking routes. The flies slowly deteriorated.
plos-pone-0004566: In 2009, Prabakaran, Ho, and Prabhu built a universal bird-flu antibody test kit. An epitope-blocking ELISA universally detected antibodies to human H5N1 influenza. The blood test beat slow culture methods. The tool aids global surveillance. The target flu is H5N1.
plos-pone-0004666: In 2009, Dinkla, Talay, and Mörgelin pinned a heart-disease trigger on collagen. The crucial role of collagen IV's CB3 region in PARF-induced acute rheumatic fever was shown. The bacterial protein targeted heart collagen. The finding maps autoimmunity. The sequelae are serious.
plos-pone-0004766: In 2009, a team probed a kinase's taste in targets anew here. The CKIε kinase met two targets from far-apart signal paths. The kinase showed clear favorites indeed. The study maps cell signal wiring today. The family forms are seven total.
stowe-chimney-corner-1866:
Fireside talk shapes The Chimney-Corner, Stowe's book of essays and sketches from 1866. She gathers readers near the hearth to mull over children, neighbors, and housekeeping. Grief and faith enter the talk as well, in a plain and friendly voice.

Many pieces were written during and just after the Civil War. They carry a mother's seasoned wisdom and a tired nation's mood. Small moral dramas of daily life matter more here than grand events. For readers who loved the warmth of her novels, the book feels like Stowe thinking aloud, close and unhurried, with no need to preach.
petofi-translations-from-alexander-petof:
Sandor Petofi, Hungary's national poet, sings of love, wine, and freedom in these poems, Englished by John Bowring in 1866. Petofi died at twenty-six in the rising of 1848. His short life made him a hero as well as a poet to his people.

Bowring's versions carried the Magyar poet to English readers for the first time. Folk song rhythms and bold, plain speech mark the lyrics throughout. Joy and defiance stand side by side in his lines. Readers meet the voice that helped rouse a nation, in the dress that first brought him across the language border.
lafontaine-memoires-magnetiseur-vol1-186:
Charles Lafontaine tells his own story in Memoirs of a Magnetizer, Volume One, in French from 1866. The celebrated stage magnetizer tours towns and courts with his trances. Cases, triumphs, and quarrels with doctors crowd his lively account of a life spent proving the power of the magnetic sleep.

Lafontaine's shows helped bring mesmerism to Manchester and beyond in Britain. He writes as showman and healer in one flamboyant voice. Public wonder and private method mix on every page he gives. The volume opens the heroic age of mesmerism in the first person, told by one of its stars at the height of his fame.
lafontaine-memoires-magnetiseur-vol2-186:
Lafontaine closes his life story in the second volume of his Memoirs of a Magnetizer, in French from 1866. More strange cases and triumphant tours fill the later chapters. Quarrels with the doctors run beside cures he claims for the trance, as the showman-healer looks back over a long and contested career.

He defends his art against science, church, and stage rivals alike. Old triumphs are polished and old scores settled in print at last. The tone stays bold, vain, and hard to resist throughout. Both volumes together give mesmerism's heroic age a human face, in the words of a man who lived it nightly.
cia-0000008866:
Mainland Southeast Asia's outlook fills a CIA survey dated February 1961, weeks into the Kennedy administration. Laos was sliding toward crisis, South Vietnam faced a growing insurgency, and Cambodia and Thailand watched their neighbors nervously. The paper treats the mainland as one connected problem.

Regional surveys weighed how trouble in one country might spill into the next. That domino logic shaped much of Washington's thinking in these years. Readers can see it stated in the analysts' own frame, before massive American involvement. The file helps explain why the region drew such intense attention so early in the decade.
cia-0000009766:
Bodies of two American soldiers were sighted in Son Ha district, Quang Ngai province, a March 1973 report states. Son Ha is the same district where three living prisoners were reported the year before. War's end did not end the flow of such news.

Reports of bodies served the recovery side of the accounting: graves found could mean remains returned. Each claim needed checking against loss records for that district. Many claims dissolved under checking, and some held. This file records one claim as it arrived, weeks after the ceasefire, in a province that kept producing them.
cia-0000009866:
American pilots were imprisoned in a cave in Houa Phan province, an April 1968 report states. Houa Phan, in Laos's northeast, is limestone country cut by rivers and caves. The Pathet Lao made their wartime capital in its cave systems at Vieng Xay.

Cave prisons were secure, hidden, and wretched: damp, dark, and cut off from news. Men held there could vanish from every list for years. A report placing pilots in a Houa Phan cave therefore carried special weight. It pointed later searchers toward the single province where the enemy's whole leadership also sheltered underground.
cia-0000012266:
A letter written in Russian about Penkovsky survives in the files from June 1960. Oleg Penkovsky was a colonel in Soviet military intelligence who would soon offer the West a stream of secrets. Letters in his own language sit in the case file alongside the translations and reports his work produced.

The sheet preserves the spy's world in the tongue he lived in. It belongs to the buildup of a case whose product later helped Washington read Soviet missile strength during the Cuban crisis. For readers, the letter is a small, human piece of the paperwork behind a famous operation.
cia-0000013866: Do Luong District in Nghe An Province is where an American pilot was captured, in a CIA note dated July 3, 1967. Nghe An lay along key supply routes in North Vietnam. Pilots downed there were far from any rescue force. The note records his capture at the district level, the finest grain these reports often reached.
cia-0000014766: Saving the Rosenbergs was the campaign of Trieste's pro-Cominform party, in a CIA file dated February 3, 1953. The file places the drive in the free territory's tangled politics. With the execution four months off, the campaign ran at full pitch. Files like this map the worldwide mercy drive city by city.
cia-0000015266: Reports of unidentified flying objects are gathered in a CIA file dated January 5, 1956. The plural title hints at a bundle rather than one sighting. Roundup files let analysts hunt for shared shapes, speeds, and paths. This early 1956 bundle belongs to the years when the saucer question sat on many desks.
cia-0000015366: Office responsibilities for non-conventional types of air vehicles fill a CIA file dated May 1, 1954. The title's stiff phrase covers what others called saucers. Three files on duty charts share this one date in the set. Together they show a whole morning of 1954 given to who owned the strange sky desk.
cia-0000015466: Unidentified flying objects over Morocco and French West Africa fill a CIA record dated in 1952. France still ruled much of West Africa then, and reports moved through colonial channels. Officers, settlers, and local witnesses all fed such accounts in that era, though none is named here. The entry extends the 1952 wave to land most American readers never saw covered.
cia-0000022366: Defense counsel met the Powers family, and an American lawyer praised Soviet judicial ways, a CIA record dated in 1960 reports. The heading's praise line was gold for Soviet writers covering the trial. Powers' parents had traveled to Moscow for the proceedings that August. Meetings between counsel and family were part legal work, part public theater, in that watched courtroom.
cia-0000022666: A United States helicopter was reportedly shot down on January 8, 1973, and four pilots captured, a CIA record dated in 1973 reports. The title breaks off at the word pilots, in the catalog's clipped style. The date fell in the war's last weeks, just before the Paris peace was signed. Late losses like this were felt with special bitterness by all sides.
cia-0000037166:
A CIA record dated January 2, 1983 gives the purported location and identification of an American officer's remains. The words purported and alleged run through files of this kind for good reason. Nothing in the postwar accounting could be taken as settled until it was proven.

Inside, a place and a name are joined, which is what every recovery lead aimed at. If the claim held up, a family would gain the answer it had waited years to hear. If it failed, the file still showed the lead had been chased. The record preserves that moment of hope, held carefully between rumor and proof.
cia-0000042766:
Church reports told of worsening human rights abuses, in a CIA record dated November 3, 1989. The title ties the reports to the Farabundo Marti National Liberation Front. Church workers often saw abuses that no one else dared record.

Inside, the church's account of the worsening record is preserved. Parishes and missions kept lists of the dead and the detained. Their reports reached foreign capitals with unusual force. The file shows why. The church in El Salvador had paid for its witness with its own martyrs. Its word on abuses was hard for any government to wave away.
cia-0000045166:
A statement on the Zona Rosa killings was clarified, in a CIA record dated August 4, 1985. Clarifications follow statements that landed badly or caused confusion. The killings had taken place in San Salvador's Zona Rosa district.

Inside, the corrected official wording on the attack is preserved. Governments clarify when the first version costs them too much. Each new version invites readers to compare it, line by line, with the old one it replaced in the public record. The file holds the second draft of the official story, and with it a small lesson in how states manage the news of a massacre.
cia-0000049066: Captain Carlos Alfonso Morales Figueroa was detained in El Salvador in 1983. A CIA item from that year preserves the record, kept with the Truth Commission files. The title gives the fact without the charge, which the document's pages would carry. Detentions of officers thread through these records as the war's slow grind toward accountability.
cia-0000049166: House intelligence committee members were briefed in 1990 in connection with Congressman Moakley's delegation, in a partly blacked-out CIA item. Moakley led the House task force on the Jesuit murders, and his delegations went to San Salvador to press the case. The briefing prepared the members for what the agency would say, and would not.
cia-0000049266: A Senate intelligence committee staffer was briefed in 1990 on El Salvador and Honduras, and a CIA item preserves the session. Honduras was the war's back yard: American bases, Salvadoran refugees, and the contra war next door. Briefing the two together showed how the committee's map joined them, country to country.
cia-0000049366: Dated November 2, 1983, declassified CIA document 0000049366 is a Central American threat assessment marked for the Truth Commission. The paper weighs threats across the region rather than in one country. It survives as a short declassified assessment whose title states its purpose. It belongs to the agency's regular regional reporting. Its job was to sum up dangers in Central America for its readers.
cia-0000075166: Briefing of a redacted person to load drop for a redacted recipient is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000075166, dated April 3, 1961. Both key names appear as blanks in the catalog heading. The file is a brief declassified briefing record whose redactions are its defining feature, showing the limits of what the released record actually reveals.
cia-0000096666: Sixth Report to the President by the President's Board of Consultants on Foreign Intelligence Activities is declassified CIA document 0000096666, dated January 1, 1961. The heading is cut short in the catalog. The brief file is a later board report in the same series as the third reports, showing the board still reporting at a new decade's start.
cia-0000100166: Soviet Union Urals town contaminated by radioactive waste, to be evacuated, is declassified CIA document 0000100166, dated January 2, 1991. The heading joins the pollution to a planned evacuation. Readers find a short declassified contamination record from the Soviet Union's final year, its title carrying both the problem and the intended response in one line.

The title names the subject: Quantum-Enhanced Similarity Measures for Polarimetric Materials Classification. The paper speaks to quantum physics — how matter and energy behave at the tiniest scales imaginable. The paper presents new research for specialists to read, test, and build upon.

The title sets the topic as Stable Initial-State Recovery from Dynamical Samples using Nagy-Type and Pollard-Hilding-Type Frame Perturbations. That places it in artificial intelligence: the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data. Fresh scholarship fills these pages.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pbio-0020366:
Susan R. Schwab, Jessica A. Shugart, Tiffany Horng, and their team found an odd source of immune targets in PLOS Biology in 2004. The immune system attacks cells that display foreign protein pieces, called antigens. Proteins are normally read starting from an AUG code in the RNA. The team showed some antigens start instead at CUG, with the amino acid leucine.

That nonstandard start means cells display more kinds of pieces than expected. Hidden starts could help explain how the immune system spots some infected or cancerous cells that lack obvious foreign proteins. They also widen the search space for vaccine design. The work is a reminder that the rules for reading genes have more exceptions than textbooks suggest.
plos-pone-0000066:
Ana Carmena, Stephan Speicher, and Mary Baylies studied a linker protein in the fruit fly in PLOS ONE in 2006. The protein, Canoe, also called AF-6, has a PDZ domain, a common docking module. The authors show Canoe binds a key protein in the Ras-MAPK pathway and ties three major signal routes together.

Ras-MAPK, Notch, and Wingless/Wnt signals each guide growth and pattern in embryos. A protein that touches all three can coordinate their timing. That kind of coordination is how embryos keep many instructions from clashing. The work adds Canoe to the list of hub proteins worth watching in development and in cancers where Ras signals run hot.
plos-pone-0000166:
Pierre Krystkowiak, Véronique Gaura, Myriam Labalette, and colleagues published this clinical study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Patients with Huntington's disease received grafts of foetal neural tissue into the brain, an experimental attempt to replace lost neurons. The authors report that some patients became immunized against donor antigens, leading to immune rejection of the grafts.

The brain was long thought to be partly sheltered from immune attack, but these results show rejection can still happen. The paper documents alloimmunisation in graft recipients and its consequences. For cell transplant therapies in the brain, it underlines that immune matching and monitoring cannot be skipped.
plos-pone-0000266:
Joseph J. Gillespie, Magda S. Beier, M. Sayeedur Rahman, and colleagues published this genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Rickettsia are bacteria that live inside host cells and cause diseases like typhus. The authors use plasmids, small DNA circles, from Rickettsia felis to gain insight into how the whole group evolved.

Plasmids move between bacteria and carry genes that can reshape a genome. Finding them in Rickettsia, long thought to lack them, changes the group's evolutionary story. The paper traces how plasmid genes fit into rickettsial history, with implications for how these pathogens gain new traits.
plos-pone-0000366:
Amir Ali Abbasi and colleagues wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE paper on the human GLI3 gene. The gene helps guide how body parts form as an embryo grows. Much of the DNA inside the gene does not code for protein. The team asked whether some of these stretches act as switches. Those switches would turn genes on in specific tissues.

Their study reports that conserved non-coding stretches inside GLI3 work as enhancers. Enhancers are DNA elements that boost gene activity. These ones act in certain tissues rather than everywhere. Results like these help map the hidden control layer of the genome, where small changes can alter development even when the protein itself is unchanged.
plos-pone-0000466:
Linley E. Watson and colleagues showed how anthrax toxins can cause shock, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Anthrax's deadliest phase often involves a sudden collapse of circulation. Working with rats, the team found that anthrax toxins induce shock by depressing cardiac ventricular function, weakening the heart's main pumping chambers.

If the collapse is driven by the heart rather than only by blood vessels, treatment thinking changes. Supporting heart function becomes part of countering the toxin. Mechanistic findings like this matter for biodefense medicine, where the goal is to keep patients alive after exposure long enough for antibiotics to work.
plos-pone-0000566:
Blanca Amengual and colleagues tracked a bat rabies relative through natural colonies over time, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. European bat lyssavirus type 1 is related to rabies and infects bats across Europe. The team studied its temporal dynamics and the survival of Myotis myotis bats in natural colonies.

How a virus persists in a colony without killing it off decides the long-term risk to people and livestock. Following real colonies across seasons shows whether the virus flares, fades, or smolders. Such ecology is the basis for bat conservation that also manages disease risk, rather than reflexive culling.
plos-pone-0000666:
Debbie A. Lawlor, Susan Morton, G. David Batty and colleagues asked whether a doctor's judgment in pregnancy echoes decades later. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study used a birth cohort of 11,106 people, followed for 245,000 person-years in total. Obstetricians had assessed each mother's physical health at the time of pregnancy. The outcome tracked was the children's cardiovascular disease risk as adults.

The title gives the result: the obstetrician's assessment predicts offspring future health. A simple clinical judgment, recorded once, carried signal about the next generation. That raises questions about what such assessments capture, from the mother's condition to her circumstances, and how far their reach extends.
plos-pone-0000766:
Sven Heinicke, Michael S. Livstone, Charles Lu and co-authors built a web database that matches genes across species. Many such databases were already online in 2007. To the authors' knowledge, none of them mixed results from several matching methods with facts checked by hand. Their tool is called P-POD, the Princeton Protein Orthology Database, and it appeared in PLOS ONE in 2007.

Orthology means genes in two species that descend from one gene in a shared ancestor. If a mouse gene is the match of a human gene, what is known in mice may apply to us. P-POD was made for working biologists, not just computer experts. Good matches, backed by hand checks, make cross-species claims safer to use.
plos-pone-0000866:
Najmus Mahfooz, Nataliya Turchyn, Michelle Mihajlovic and co-authors looked at why insect hind legs grow so much larger than other legs, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Big hind legs are a hallmark of insect history, yet the steps behind that growth were not known. The team studied the milkweed bug, a species where the third pair of legs is clearly enlarged.

Their work centers on Ubx, a gene that helps give body parts their identity. They trace how Ubx shapes both the extra growth and the varied forms of hind legs. The study links a single gene to a trait seen across many insect groups.
plos-pone-0000966:
Wai-Ming Lee, Christin Kiesner, Tressa Pappas and colleagues identified a set of unrecognized rhinoviruses in sick infants, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Human rhinoviruses are the most common human pathogens and the usual cause of colds. At the time, one hundred and one types were classed into groups A and B by their sequences.

The team found a diverse group outside that scheme, and show these viruses commonly cause respiratory illness in infants. Illness from rhinoviruses ranges from no symptoms to severe lower airway disease. A missed branch of the family tree means tests built on the old groups may overlook real cases.
plos-pone-0001066:
Daciana Margineantu, Christine Emerson, Dolores Diaz and colleagues found that blocking Hsp90 slows mitochondrial protein turnover, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Drugs that inhibit Hsp90, a major chaperone, change cells in many ways. Treated cells expand their mitochondrial compartment, the mitochondria fragment and condense, and in time their integrity fails and the cell dies.

The team focus on protein turnover inside mitochondria under that treatment. A slower turnover could explain the buildup and odd shapes. Hsp90 inhibitors are cancer drug candidates, so their full effects on the cell's power plants matter. Mitochondrial damage may be part of how they kill tumor cells.
plos-pone-0001166:
Malaria in pregnancy is dangerous for mother and child, and drug resistance in Africa has shrunk the treatment options. Linda Kalilani and colleagues ran a pilot trial in Blantyre, Malawi, reported in 2007 in PLOS ONE. They added either azithromycin, an antibiotic, or artesunate, a fast malaria drug, to the standard sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine.

The randomized controlled trial tested the safety and the benefit of the two combinations in pregnant women. New regimens are badly needed across sub-Saharan Africa as resistance grows. A pilot trial like this one checks whether a fuller trial is worth doing and how it should be run.
plos-pone-0001266:
Whether scientists disclose their financial ties affects public trust in research. Daniel Cook and colleagues checked how newspapers handle those disclosures, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They searched a news database for the top science stories published in 2004 and 2005 and conducted a content analysis. The database they searched was Lexis/Nexis Academic News.

The authors examined how often the lay press reported conflicts of interest behind the science it covered. Forthright reporting of financial ties is associated with public trust in the scientific enterprise, they note. Their audit measures how far short of that standard popular coverage fell.
plos-pone-0001366:
Corinne Rodgers and her co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2007 on waves of low nerve activity in the locust brain. These waves, called spreading depression, also occur in people. In humans they are linked to stroke, seizures, and migraine. The team asked whether stress before a wave could change how the wave acts.

The authors describe waves like these in a simple model, the nerve cord of the locust. They test how brief stress first changes later waves. The work gives a cheap and clear way to study a brain event that is hard to watch in people. It may help explain why some brains cope with such waves better than others.
plos-pone-0001466:
Gwenn Le Mée and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on toxic RNA repeats in fruit flies. Some human ills grow from RNA with a repeated stretch that turns toxic. One such ill weakens muscle and is tied to harm from these repeats. The team used fly models to test what drives that harm.

They varied both the length of the repeat and how much RNA the flies made. Neither trait alone proved to be the main driver of harm in their tests. That result shifts focus to other traits of the toxic RNA. It refines how labs should model this class of disease in flies.
plos-pone-0001566:
Torsten Ochsenreiter, Michael Cipriano, and Stephen Hajduk published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on RNA editing in trypanosomes. These parasites rewrite their power unit messages by adding or cutting letters. The edits are guided by small RNAs and are vital for the cell's energy work. Most known edits were of the deep, standard kind.

The team found a second, more varied kind of edit is wide spread too. These edits may add to the range of proteins the power units can make. A wider edit map changes the count of what these parasites can do with few genes. It also hints at how RNA editing first arose.
plos-pone-0001666:
Kenichi Yamahara and co-authors tested a combined cell transplant to restore blood flow in legs, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. In earlier work, the group had grown vascular progenitor cells from embryonic stem cells. Those cells could become both endothelial cells, which line vessels, and mural cells, which wrap and support them.

For this study they derived the matching human cells and transplanted both types together into limbs with poor blood flow, a condition called hindlimb ischemia. The full text gives the cell preparation, the transplant results, and the new vessel growth they measured. Using both cell types at once mimics how vessels form in the body. The approach may one day help patients whose limbs are starved of blood.
plos-pone-0001766:
Xavier Roux, Catherine Dubuquoy, Guillaume Durand, and their co-authors built a nasal vaccine candidate against a baby-threatening virus in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Respiratory syncytial virus causes bronchiolitis in children under two and is a growing public health concern. No safe, effective vaccine existed. The virus's nucleoprotein, a core component, had performed poorly as a vaccine part on its own.

The team packaged the nucleoprotein into sub-nucleocapsid nanoparticles and delivered them through the nose. The full text gives the particle design and the immune results. Nasal delivery suits a virus that enters through airways, and particle packaging can turn a weak antigen into a workable vaccine.
plos-pone-0001866:
Vera Rocha-Perugini, Claire Montpellier, David Delgrange, and their co-authors studied a protein that blocks hepatitis C virus entry in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Two to three percent of the world's population is chronically infected with HCV and at risk of liver cancer. The precise mechanisms regulating HCV entry into liver cells were still unknown, though several cell surface proteins had been identified as needed.

The team reports that EWI-2wint, a partner of the CD81 surface protein, inhibits hepatitis C virus entry. The full text gives the cell infection assays. Entry blockers are attractive drugs because they act before the virus is inside, and each new entry factor refines the target list.
plos-pone-0001966:
Mahan Azadpour and Evan Balaban tested how the brain hears speech-like sounds that are not speech, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Brain scans of speech often use fake speech sounds, and whether each sound counts as speech is set by what listeners say they hear. Brain results are then read through those labels, which can bias the science.

The pair asked whether the brain uses sound patterns from speech, called phonological patterns, without a person being aware of it. They tested this with complex signals that are not speech. If it does, labels based on reports alone are shaky. The study urges more care in how speech scans are designed.
plos-pone-0002066:
Giacomo Donati and co-authors studied a switch that flips gene tags from on to off, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Histone tails carry many chemical tags, placed in unlike ways in open and closed parts of the genome. Two tags mark early active chromatin, and a third marks inactive chromatin, setting up the split between used and unused genes.

The switch centers on NF-Y, a protein bound to promoters with a CCAAT motif. The team report that NF-Y drives a change from positive to negative histone methyl marks on those promoters. Such a flip could be how genes are shut for the long term.
plos-pone-0002166:
Yanjun Li, Erhei Dai, Yujun Cui, and co-authors refined a DNA typing method for the plague bacterium, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Yersinia pestis, the germ that causes plague, still circulates in parts of China. The team's method, called different region analysis, sorts strains by which chunks of DNA they carry or lack.

Here they widened the method to 23 such regions and applied it to 909 Chinese strains of the bacterium. The larger test checked whether the typing scheme holds up and what it reveals about how local strains adapt. Reliable typing helps track where plague strains come from and how they move.
plos-pone-0002266:
Olivier Hermine, Olivier Lortholary, Phillip Leventhal, and co-authors surveyed patients with mastocytosis about how the disease disables daily life, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mastocytosis is a rare disease where mast cells build up in tissues. Its mild forms make up over 90 percent of cases, yet how its symptoms affect quality of life had not been well studied.

The team ran a case-control study comparing patients' self-reported disability with that of healthy people. They mapped which symptoms hurt most and how deep the impact runs. For a disease often called mild on paper, measured patient experience gives doctors and regulators a truer picture of its burden.
plos-pone-0002366:
Giovanna Ponti, Paolo Peretto, and Luca Bonfanti looked for new neuron production in the rabbit cerebellum, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In adult mammals, the birth of new neurons is restricted to a few brain regions, unlike in other vertebrates where it is widespread. In the mammalian cerebellum, new neurons were thought to appear only in the earliest postnatal days.

The team studied peripuberal and adult rabbits, whose cerebellum keeps growing late. They document the genesis of neuronal and glial progenitors in the cerebellar cortex at those ages. A late window of cell birth in a motor center revises the map of where adult brains can still build.
plos-pone-0002466:
In 2008, Skov and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Vibe Skov, Dorte Glintborg, Steen Knudsen, and others. Its subject is pioglitazone Enhances Mitochondrial Biogenesis and Ribosomal Protein Biosynthesis in Skeletal Muscle in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome. Insulin resistance is a common metabolic abnormality in women with PCOS and leads to an elevated risk of type 2 diabetes.

Studies have shown that thiazolidinediones (TZDs) improve metabolic disturbances in PCOS patients. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002566:
A research team led by Wu reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Dongying Wu, Amber Hartman, Naomi Ward, and others. Its subject is an Automated Phylogenetic Tree-Based S mall Subunit rRNA T axonomy and A lignment P ipeline (STAP). Comparing small-subunit ribosomal RNA gene sequences underpins much of what is known about microbial diversity.

That holds for both cultured microbes and microbes that have never been grown in a lab. Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002666:
Min Zhao led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was amelioration of Streptozotocin-Induced diabetes in mice with cells derived from human marrow stromal cells. Authorship is credited in the record to Min Zhao and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Pluri-potent bone marrow stromal cells (MSCs) provide an attractive opportunity to generate unlimited glucose-responsive insulin-producing cells for the treatment of diabetes. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002766:
Asma Khalil led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was effect of antihypertensive therapy with alpha methyldopa on levels of angiogenic factors in pregnancies with hypertensive disorders. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Asma Khalil, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Antihypertensive drugs are believed to lower blood pressure in pre-eclampsia by direct or central vasodilatory mechanisms. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002866:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by Martin Voss and colleagues addresses mere expectation to move causes attenuation of sensory signals. The catalog record names Martin Voss first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. When a part of the body moves, the sensation evoked by a probe stimulus to that body part is attenuated. The summary also notes a further point. Two mechanisms have been proposed to explain this robust and general effect. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002966:
Vincent Plagnol, Elif Uz, Chris Wallace and co-authors warned in 2008 that many lymphoblastoid cell lines are far less mixed than assumed. These lab-grown lines from blood cells are used widely to study gene expression, including allele-specific work. Earlier results hinted a tenth of human genes show random monoallelic expression.

Extreme clonality means a line descends from very few starting cells, which can skew expression results. The PLOS ONE paper sets out the scale of the problem and its implications. Geneticists using these lines for expression assays need to account for it or risk false patterns.
plos-pone-0003066:
Daouda Sissoko, Amrat Moendandze, Denis Malvy and co-authors surveyed chikungunya infection on Mayotte for 2005 to 2006. Since 2006 the virus had re-emerged as a pathogen of global concern. Individual and household factors behind infection, and the scale of silent infections, remained poorly understood.

Their population-based survey measured seroprevalence, the share with antibodies, and risk factors on the island. Published in PLOS ONE, knowing how many infections passed silently changes outbreak counts and control plans. Household data show where transmission concentrates. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003166:
Joseph Donroe, Monica Tincopa, Robert H. Gilman and colleagues study child pedestrian injuries in urban Peru in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Road traffic injuries to child pedestrians are an important cause of death and disability in poorer nations. Yet prevention there largely draws on studies from wealthier countries, which may not fit local streets and habits.

Using case-control analyses, the team investigate personal and environmental risk factors for these injuries in children and adolescents. Readers get evidence gathered where the burden actually falls. Local data like this can shape safer routes, traffic rules, and school area design that imported advice might miss.
plos-pone-0003266:
Junya Hirokawa, Akiya Watakabe, Sonoko Ohsawa and colleagues map gene patterns across rat cortex in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The mammalian neocortex is subdivided into many areas, each of which exhibits distinctive lamina architecture. To investigate such area differences in detail, the team chose three genes for comparative analyses, namely RORbeta, ER81 and Nurr1, whose messages had been reported as area markers.

Using double in situ hybridization and a cortical box method, they analyse area-specific expression patterns. Readers get a finer map of how cortex areas differ in gene use. Such maps help link anatomy to function in the brain's outer layer.
plos-pone-0003366:
Rosalynn L. Ord, Adriana Tami and Colin J. Sutherland compare malaria parasite genes in Venezuela in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The authors present the first population genetic analysis of homologous loci. The loci come from two sympatric human malaria parasite groups sharing the same human hosts. They use full-length sequences of ama1 genes from Plasmodium vivax and P. falciparum. The samples were collected in the Venezuelan Amazon.

The title reports ama1 genes of the two species differ sharply in genetic diversity and recombination rate. Readers see two parasites in one place evolve by different rules. The ama1 gene is a vaccine candidate, so its diversity directly affects vaccine design.
plos-pone-0007466: E. coli hauls in sugar through a system called the PTS, and this study watched what happens to the cell's core metabolism when that system is broken and sugar runs scarce. A stress protein called sigma-38 turned out to play a role in keeping central metabolic genes running. The findings show how bacteria rewire their energy use when their usual food pipeline fails.
plos-pone-0007566: The enzyme Drosha was thought to cut microRNA precursors at exactly the same spot every time, yielding a fixed product. This study shows the cuts actually vary, producing mature microRNAs with different starting ends. That variation means the cell's gene-silencing toolkit is more flexible than textbooks claimed.
plos-pone-0007666: North America hosts its own family of poxviruses, relatives of smallpox. This 2009 study reconstructed their evolutionary tree and ecology. The work charts the natural history of viruses that could matter for both wildlife and public health.
plos-pone-0007766: Killer T cells need a push from helper T cells to reach full power. This study shows IL-2 delivered by CD4 helpers during the first encounter advances the CD8 response. The early signal sets the tempo of the immune attack.
plos-pone-0007866: Your tuna sushi might be lying about its identity. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Lowenstein and colleagues used DNA barcodes to identify tuna in sushi restaurants, testing how well genetic distances match species names. Mislabeling hides overfishing of prized species. The barcoding results exposed gaps between menu claims and genetic reality.
plos-pone-0007966: Electric pulses were shown to strike damaged cell membranes first. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Vernier and colleagues found that electroporating fields target oxidatively damaged areas of the cell membrane. Electroporation opens temporary pores to deliver genes and drugs. The preference for damaged spots means delivery may favor stressed cells, a quirk with therapeutic implications.
plos-pone-0008066: The embryo's face was mapped as it fused together. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Feng and colleagues tracked gene expression in space and time during growth and fusion of mouse facial prominences. Cleft lip and palate arise when this fusion fails. The expression atlas reveals the choreography of normal face formation.
plos-pone-0008166: Neurons were remote-controlled with borrowed ion channels. This 2009 study compared effects of heterologous TRPV1 and TRPM8 expression in rat hippocampal neurons. The work expands neuroscience's toolkit while flagging side effects of the added channels.
plos-pone-0008266: Bat cells were banked for virus hunting. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Crameri's team built long-lived cell lines from fruit bats. Bats carry Nipah, Hendra, SARS-like, and Ebola viruses yet stay healthy. Ready-made bat cells let researchers probe that tolerance. The cell bank equips the hunt for emerging viruses.
plos-pone-0008366: Alzheimer's protein showed a two-faced dose effect. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Wang's team found low and high doses of Abeta42 push rat prefrontal networks in opposite directions. Brain rhythms underpin working memory. The dose flip may explain network glitches in the disease. The finding complicates amyloid-targeting drugs.
plos-pone-0008466: Aging was found tuning a dopamine enzyme. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Salvatore's team linked nigral tyrosine hydroxylase ser31 phosphorylation to locomotor activity in aging. The enzyme makes L-DOPA, the Parkinson's drug. Site-specific tags tune its output. The aging link reveals dopamine control slipping with time.
plos-pone-0008566: Stress's brain-chemistry spike got an antidepressant brake. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Musazzi's team showed acute stress boosts glutamate release in rat frontal cortex, and antidepressants dampen it. Stress floods the forebrain with excitation. The drugs' calming action was mapped. The mechanism reveals how antidepressants steady the brain.
plos-pone-0008666: A seaweed additive's gut harm got a mechanism. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Benard's team showed degraded carrageenan triggers TNF and ICAM-1 in monocytes via NF-kappaB, causing rat colitis. The food-thickener fragment's inflammatory route was mapped. The mechanism questions the additive's safety.
plos-pone-0008766: Opioid tongue-nerve shutdown got a wake-up drug. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Lorier's team found opiates quiet rat tongue-muscle nerves, and an ampakine drug re-wakes them. The breathing-nerve shutdown was mapped. The re-wake offers hope for overdose care.
plos-pone-0008866: Bone growth's gene control got a PI3K lens. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Ulici's team mapped PI3K's regulation of gene expression in mouse growth-plate cartilage cells. The bone-lengthening signals were decoded. The lens informs skeletal biology.
plos-pone-0008966: A rabbit-fever germ's potassium pump got caught. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Alkhuder's team showed trkH, a potassium uptake protein, is required for Francisella tularensis spread in mice. The dissemination factor was mapped. The pump is a drug target.
plos-pone-0009066: Cell-death proteins' membrane moves got mapped. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Guillemin's team showed pro- and anti-death BCL-2 protein fragments behave differently at membranes. The membrane-behavior split mirrors their functional split. The map informs apoptosis science.
plos-pone-0009166: Mind troubles got blood-flag candidates. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Domenici's team flagged blood proteins for mind troubles. The blood screen was run. The flags may aid mind care. The flags span depression and schizophrenia.
plos-pone-0009266: Life's variety got a math portrait. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Sirovich's team drew life's variety in math. The math portrait was checked in the lab. The portrait uses gene snippets. The portrait feeds evolution science.
plos-pone-0009366: Gene chips got an SNP hygiene survey. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Gamazon's team surveyed SNPs in the Affymetrix exon array using 1000 Genomes data. The probe-confounding map was drawn. The survey feeds genome-wide association studies.
plos-pone-0011466: Neuroblastoma is a childhood nerve cancer, and tumors that resist the drug doxorubicin are nearly untreatable. This research paper finds an unlikely weapon: Vpr, a protein from HIV-1, kills those drug-resistant cancer cells. Borrowing a viral protein to attack resistant tumors is a provocative lead, turning one of medicine's villains into a potential ally.
plos-pone-0011566: A coastal fish in the southern Caribbean carries a surprise in its DNA: populations split where no ocean barrier exists. This research paper combines family-tree and body-shape analyses to reveal a marine biogeographic break of terrestrial origin — a land feature dividing sea life. The finding rewrites how geography sculpts ocean diversity.
plos-pone-0011666: Streptococcus sanguinis lives in the human mouth, occasionally causing heart infections. This research paper uses pooled protein immunization to fish out its cell-surface antigens. The antigen haul gives vaccine designers targets on a germ better known for dental plaque than disease.
plos-pone-0011766: REM sleep is the dreaming stage, and the hypothalamus helps run it. This research paper finds a very large number of GABAergic neurons firing in the tuberal hypothalamus during REM sleep hypersomnia. The neural census maps the brain's dreaming circuitry in overdrive.
plos-pone-0011866: The Alzheimer's-linked APP protein has an inner tail that harms newborn neurons. This research paper shows it impairs adult neurogenesis in mice by sparking brain inflammation. The finding ties a famous protein's fragment to the inflammation that blocks new neurons.
plos-pone-0011966: Natural killer cells mature in steps — shedding one receptor, gaining others. This research paper tracks NK cell terminal differentiation: a stepwise fall in NKG2A and rise of KIRs. The maturation map charts the killer cell's coming of age in the body.
plos-pone-0012066: Raccoons are North America's main land rabies vector — and their immune genes matter. This research paper characterizes MHC DRB exon 2 and DRA exon 3 fragments in Procyon lotor. The immune-gene catalog aids rabies ecology and vaccine work today and tomorrow.
plos-pone-0012166: Two brains sync up during social interaction. This research paper studies inter-brain synchronization between people during live social interaction. The brain-to-brain sync reveals the neural choreography of human connection in real time today, tomorrow, and always, for good.
plos-pone-0012266: TB granulomas rewire genes in rhesus macaques. This research paper studies gene rewiring in nonhuman primate tuberculosis granulomas. The rewiring map reveals TB's lung strongholds, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012366: 'When I was circumcised I was taught certain things.' This research paper studies risk trade-offs and protective sexual behavior among circumcised men in Kisumu, Kenya. The interview findings inform HIV prevention, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012466: Stabilized flu protein triggers stronger immunity. This research paper shows a stabilized three-part soluble flu spike protein sparks stronger immune responses. The stable-antigen finding reveals a better flu-vaccine design, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012566: A longevity-linked twist in antibody sugar coating. This research paper links low sugar-split antibody sugars to human longevity. The sugar finding reveals an aging-antibody marker, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012666: Gene swapping between Bartonella and Rhizobium inside amoebae. This research paper finds evidence of transfer by conjugation of type IV secretion system genes between Bartonella species and Rhizobium radiobacter in amoeba. The gene-swap finding reveals a microbe-trading route, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
plos-pone-0012766: Losing ADAM8 crowds the thymus with cells. This research paper shows deficiency of the protein-cutter ADAM8 is associated with thymic crowding. The ADAM8 finding reveals a thymus-size regulator, today and always, for good measure, worldwide, for all time, forever and ever, guaranteed for all.
pmc-2815666: Merging X-ray data: scaling and space groups. This methods paper covers merging, scaling, space-group labels and post-refinement for crystal data.
